finding: Relative yield loss = ky x relative shortfall in crop water use. Seasonal ky for maize is 1.25 (bean 1.15, potato 1.10, winter wheat 1.00, sunflower 0.95, cotton 0.85, soybean 0.85, groundnut 0.70). The relation originates in FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 33 (S-FAO33).
Maize rainfall limits: absolute minimum 400 mm, optimum 600-1200 mm, absolute maximum 1800 mm. Kept for comparison; the stress levels use Concern (E-0003).
note: EcoCrop gives limits, not yield.

finding: Maize needs between 500 and 1200 mm over the cycle; short-season varieties withstand a minimum of 300 mm. Optimal air temperature 18-32 C.
note: Gives requirements; the only quantified yield loss is for delayed planting.

finding: Suitability classes can be related to relative yield, e.g. s1 = 1.0-0.8, s2 = 0.8-0.7, s3 = 0.7-0.6 of the best yield, 'but not necessarily these values'. Stated as examples only.
note: Supports reading suitability as relative yield only loosely.

finding: General rule for drought. Stress levels are season rainfall below 100 %, 80 % and 60 % of the crop's requirement; for maize 500, 400 and 300 mm, which are Concern's requirement and withstand-minimum (E-0003) and match the Atlas generic thresholds. The same fractions are applied to other crops. Central loss = 1.25 x rainfall shortfall (E-0001) at the middle of each band: moderate 12 %, severe 38 %, extreme 62 % (taken at half the requirement). Lower bound: top of the band under the same rule. Upper bound: middle of the band if yield fell in a straight line from the requirement to zero at 60 % of it. Derived for maize; applied to all crops until deep dives are done.
note: Assumes shortfall in crop water use is proportional to shortfall in season rainfall. Ignores timing within the season.

finding: Each degree day spent above 30 C reduced the final yield by 1 % under optimal rain-fed conditions and by 1.7 % under drought (more than 20,000 trials, 1999-2007). Model: log(yield) with station and year fixed effects; coefficients -0.01 and -0.017 per degree day above 30 C. Degree days are hourly temperatures interpolated between daily Tmin and Tmax with a sine curve, summed from sowing to 150 days after sowing.
unit: change in log yield per degree day above 30 C
locator: p. 42 abstract; p. 43 eq. 1 and text; p. 45 Methods eq. 2; SI Fig. S1 (degree days 0 to about 120)
note: Full text read 24 Nov 2026. Trials were well fertilised; the authors note nitrogen stress mutes heat response, so low-input farms may lose less. Sensitivity is highest around silking (SI Fig. S3).

finding: General rule for heat (v2.1, decision 0001, amended 24 Nov 2026). Loss = 1 - exp(-0.01 x degree days above the crop's moderate threshold, summed over its heat window), Lobell's log-yield form (E-0006); upper value with -0.017. Degree days per level from E-0123: central at the median, lower at the 25th percentile, upper at the 75th. Result: moderate 8 % (5-20), severe 34 % (19-65), extreme 64 % (50-95). Cross-check: 52-75 % kernel loss after heat at silking (E-0124). Derived for maize; applied to all crops until deep dives are done.
note: v2 (23 Nov) used 1 % x degree days, capped at 75 %; the log form follows the source and needs no cap. Interim: degree days are from Kenya only, with an assumed daily range.

finding: Conservation agriculture raised yield by 3.7 % across six major crop species against conventional tillage (933 observations, 16 countries).
note: First pass: read from the abstract only. Conservation agriculture is wider than reduced tillage with residue.

finding: Maize: 4.0 % against conventional tillage; 8.4 % where the conservation agriculture principles were combined.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: 'The largest yield benefits from CA occur in combination with low rainfall and herbicides.' Direction only; no size.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: Performance of conservation agriculture relative to conventional practice 'improves with increasing drought severity or exposure to high temperatures'. In very wet seasons and on clay-rich soils it yields less. Direction only in the abstract.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only. Tropics and subtropics with a sub-Saharan Africa focus. Effect sizes are in the full text.

finding: As E-0104 for high temperatures. Moisture and heat stress effects are non-additive and depend on soil clay content.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: 'Mulching performed better when the rainfall is <600 mm.' Maize, millet and sorghum in Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Senegal; 63 reports. Direction only.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only. Mulching is taken as soil cover; it is not a cover crop.

finding: Mean effects of the practices on cereal yield were 'more positive than negative except with parkland trees'. No size given in the abstract.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: Coppicing trees and rotations improved yields where rainfall is above 800 mm; 'the opposite happens with parkland and soil-water conservation measures', i.e. parklands do relatively better at lower rainfall. Direction only.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: Agroforestry 'significantly increased crop yield' against plots without trees (yield subset: 397 observations from 61 publications in 17 countries). Size not in the abstract.
note: Covers agroforestry as a whole, not parklands alone. Results section not read.

finding: As E-0109; applies to tree-crop intercropping as part of agroforestry as a whole.
note: Results section not read.

finding: Coppicing woody legumes raised maize yield by 1.6 t/ha over unfertilised maize (non-coppicing 1.3 t/ha). Doubling or tripling of yield occurred only on low and medium potential sites. 94 publications.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only. Absolute gain, not a percentage.

finding: Herbaceous green manure legumes raised maize yield by 0.8 t/ha over unfertilised maize. 94 publications.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only. Absolute gain, not a percentage.

finding: Biochar gave 'a 25% average increase in yield in the tropics' and no effect in temperate regions; 13 % across all studies. About 1,100 comparisons from about 110 studies. Gains highest on low-pH soils.
note: Tropics defined as within 35 degrees of the equator; not Africa-specific.

finding: Alternate wetting and drying lowered rice yield by 5.4 % overall against continuous flooding. Mild AWD: yields 'not significantly reduced in most circumstances'. Severe AWD: -22.6 %. 56 studies, 528 comparisons.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: 'Cocoa yields in agroforestry systems were 25% lower than in monocultures, but total system yields were about ten times higher.' 52 articles.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: Agroforestry contributes to climate adaptation by 'lowering mean temperatures and buffering temperature extremes'. No yield effect under heat is given.
note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: Milk yield rose by 39 % with improved legume feeding against basal diets (72 observations). 72 studies, 780 treatment-control pairs, 15 countries. No rainfall or temperature moderator analysed.
locator: abstract and first half of text
note: Not a full meta-analysis: variances often unreported. On-station yields are not reached by most farmers.

note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

note: First pass: read from the abstract only.

finding: Silicate rock powders gave a 33 % yield gain against matched controls in Brazil (54 studies). About 80 % of observations are greenhouse, pot or incubation trials.
note: Brazil only; mostly pot trials. A field-only figure exists in the paper but was not confirmed.

finding: Yields increase with temperature up to 29 C for corn, 30 C for soybeans and 32 C for cotton, and temperatures above these thresholds are very harmful; the slope above the optimum is much steeper than below it. Degree days use the whole distribution of temperature within each day.
note: United States county yields. Supports a steep loss above a per-crop threshold, so a degree-day base per crop; the threshold values themselves are US-specific.

finding: Degree days above 30 C in the maize heat window, single-sine method with an assumed 12 C daily range, Kenya cube (CHIRTS-ERA5), two sowing dates, with and without a 3 C warm-offset correction. Across the four runs: moderate p25 5.1 / median 8.6 / p75 13.3; severe 21.4 / 42.1 / 62.3; extreme 70.1 / 100.9 / 180 (smallest p25, median of the medians, largest p75). Counted from the daily maximum alone the values are 4-5 times higher.
unit: degree days above the moderate threshold
note: Interim. Kenya only, all land cells (no crop mask), fixed sowing dates, assumed daily range, day rules not agreed. To be replaced by pipeline output once it reads daily minimum temperature. Script: OneDrive Technical Development/Adaptation & Production Benefits/Stress tiers and heat loss/scripts/heat_dd_by_tier.py.

finding: Daytime heating to about 33-40 C at ear level for 15 days cut harvestable kernels by a mean of 51.8 % just before silking and 74.5 % during silking, across temperate, tropical and crossed hybrids in two field experiments.
note: Argentina field experiments. Kernel number, not yield; one ear per plant. Cross-check for the extreme heat loss (64 % central under the log-yield rule).

finding: Meta-regression of the CA-to-conventional maize yield ratio (1042 observations, 85 sites, 1984-2013; 84.7 % south-east Africa). Moisture stress is the growing-season precipitation balance (rainfall minus Penman-Monteith PET) of each observed season. CA yields are generally higher where the balance is below 200 mm, and the advantage grows as the season gets drier.
unit: mm precipitation balance below which CA generally outyields conventional
note: Response ratio only, from a continuous surface: not m. The supplement holds the meta-dataset (B.1) and the bootstrapped coefficients (Table A.6), from which arm-level stress contrasts could be re-derived in phase 2. Stress is measured per season, not by site climate.

finding: Heat stress is growing degree days above 30 C around anthesis, as ln(GDD30+ + 1). Under drought, CA increasingly outperforms conventional practice as heat stress rises. With a rainfall surplus, rising heat reduces CA's relative performance, which turns negative on clay-rich soils. Heat and moisture effects are non-additive and depend on clay content.
note: Direction and shape only; values are read from a figure surface (soil clay set at 25 % in Figs 3-4).

finding: In very wet seasons and on clay-rich soils (clay above 50 %), CA yields less than conventional practice; the authors attribute this to waterlogging.
note: Excess-rainfall finding: hazard left blank (the tables cover drought and heat only). Relevant to the sign of m in wet seasons.

finding: Under high heat stress, the relative yield benefit of CA narrows as more nitrogen is applied to both systems, but stays positive even at very high N rates. With little heat stress (under 1 GDD30+), more N improves CA's relative performance.
note: Shown for a 154 mm rainfall surplus and 25 % clay. A moderator to carry into strata, not a separate value.

finding: Full CA, with crop diversification, changed less under heat stress than no-till or reduced tillage with cover alone. Without diversification, rising heat and falling precipitation balance increasingly improved CA's relative performance.
note: Diversification is a stability moderator: decide in phase 2 whether to stratify C2.2 by it.

finding: CA vs conventional tillage yield across crops at sites with average seasonal rainfall below 400 mm (24 observations, 5 studies).
note: The strata are classes of the site's average seasonal rainfall, not stressed seasons, so this is a dry-climate contrast, not m. The open dataset (CIRAD 10.18167/DVN1/DLTQWR) records actual seasonal rainfall for each row, so a season-level re-analysis is possible in phase 2.

finding: As E-0306, at sites with 400-800 mm average seasonal rainfall (431 observations, 48 studies).
note: Site climate class; see E-0306.

finding: As E-0306, at sites with 800-1,200 mm average seasonal rainfall (375 observations, 45 studies).
note: Reference class for the drier strata. The effect here is significantly lower than below 400 mm (P < 0.05).

finding: As E-0306, at sites with more than 1,200 mm average seasonal rainfall (103 observations, 9 studies): yields lower under CA.
note: Wet-climate finding; hazard blank. Consistent with E-0303.

finding: Rainfall interacts with soil texture. Below 800 mm seasonal rainfall, CA outyielded CT on all soil types. At 800-1,200 mm it did so only on coarse soils (4.7 %, CI 2.8-6.7). Above 1,200 mm the effect was negative on medium and fine soils and zero on sandy soils.
unit: percent yield change (CA vs CT), coarse soils, 800-1,200 mm
note: Soil texture is a moderator for C2.2 strata (with Steward 2018 clay content, E-0302).

finding: Langgewens dryland wheat LTE, 1976-2020 (395 mm mean annual rainfall, about 80 % in April-September). Over 1996-2020, seasonal rainfall explained 37 % of wheat yield variation under mouldboard ploughing and 21 % under the infrequent shallow-tine then no-till sequence. Yields fell with seasonal rainfall until 2013 but not afterwards.
unit: percent of yield variance explained by seasonal rainfall (R2)
note: Lower R2 under reduced tillage is a hint of buffering, not a stress contrast. Yearly yields are plotted as 4-year rolling means (Fig. 3); single years only for 2014, 2016, 2018 and 2020 (Fig. 4). Preprint, not peer reviewed. Season-level arm yields need the WCDoA data (request pending Pete's go).

Yearly arm yields: p. 22, Fig. 2 (graph only: per site, 4 arms UC, UC+BC, FC, FC+BC, every season); p. 23, Table 2 (biochar increment per season pooled across sites and fertiliser). Seasons: 10 maize, 8 soybean (SR2006-LR2016); 3 replicate blocks per site, 3 sites.

note: Per-season increments (Mg/ha, SE): SR2006 0.55 (0.29); LR2007 0.77 (0.30); LR2008 2.93 (0.54); LR2009 1.68 (0.32); LR2010 0.82; LR2011 0.89; LR2012 0.83; LR2014 1.00; LR2015 0.79; LR2016 1.44. note: Table 3 maize SD of season random effect (Mg/ha): UC 0.75, UC+BC 0.63, FC 0.89, FC+BC 1.05 (SD higher with biochar under fertiliser; CV lower because mean is higher).
